What is the difference between an EMR and an EHR?

An EMR is the digital version of one practice's paper chart, used mostly inside that organization. An EHR covers the same clinical data but is designed to follow the patient across providers through standards-based exchange (FHIR, C-CDA, HIE connections, patient portals). In practice products are called both. 💡 Mention interoperability as the deciding difference.
What is OpenEMR and what is its tech stack?

OpenEMR is an open-source (GPL), ONC-certified EHR and practice-management system. It covers demographics, encounters, clinical forms, scheduling, billing, e-prescribing integrations, lab interfaces and a patient portal. It runs on PHP with MySQL/MariaDB behind Apache, is often deployed with the official Docker images, mixes legacy procedural code with namespaced src/ classes and Twig templates, and offers REST and FHIR R4 APIs secured with OAuth2/SMART.
How do you customize OpenEMR without breaking upgrades?

Configure before you code: globals, layout-based forms, lists, ACLs, menus. For code, build a custom module that hooks into core through Symfony EventDispatcher events and keeps its own namespace, tables and install/upgrade SQL. Reuse core helpers for DB access, escaping, CSRF and ACL checks. Unavoidable core patches should be small, documented and sent upstream where possible. Test every upgrade on a staging copy. 💡 Keeping a list of "core diffs we carry" makes upgrades predictable.
How does OpenEMR support multiple tenants?

Through multisite. Each site lives under sites/<siteid>/ with its own sqlconf.php, configuration and document storage, and usually its own database. The site ID appears in API and OAuth paths (/apis/<site>/fhir). That is database-per-tenant isolation: good for PHI separation and per-tenant restore, with the trade-off that schema upgrades and onboarding have to be automated across all sites.
Compare database-per-tenant with shared-schema tenancy for a healthcare SaaS.

Database per tenant gives strong isolation and simple per-tenant backup and deletion, and it is easier to explain to auditors, but there are more databases to migrate and monitor. Shared schema with tenant_id is cheaper and simpler to run, but a single missing WHERE tenant_id = ? leaks PHI. If you choose it, enforce the filter centrally (repository layer or row-level security) and test for it. For PHI, many teams accept the operational cost of database-per-tenant.
HL7 v2 vs FHIR — when would you use each?

HL7 v2 is pipe-delimited, event-driven messaging (ADT, ORM/OML, ORU) over MLLP. It remains the standard for in-hospital feeds such as lab results and admissions, often routed through an interface engine. FHIR is resource-based REST/JSON with OAuth2, suited to apps, patient access, payer APIs and regulatory requirements. Real systems often use both: v2 feeds come in, are mapped to FHIR resources, and are exposed through a FHIR API.
Name key FHIR resources and what they represent.

Patient (demographics), Practitioner/Organization (providers), Encounter (a visit), Condition (problem/diagnosis), Observation (vitals, labs, smoking status), MedicationRequest (prescription), AllergyIntolerance, Immunization, Procedure, DiagnosticReport, DocumentReference, Appointment. They link by references, e.g. an Observation's subject → Patient and encounter → Encounter.
How does FHIR search work? Give examples.

Search is GET [base]/[Type]?params and returns a searchset Bundle with paging links. Each resource defines its own parameters, and prefixes and modifiers refine them.
GET /Patient?family=doe&birthdate=ge1980-01-01
GET /Observation?patient=123&code=http://loinc.org|8867-4&_sort=-date&_count=10
GET /MedicationRequest?patient=123&status=active&_include=MedicationRequest:medication
GET /Encounter?patient=123&date=ge2026-01-01&_revinclude=Observation:encounter
💡 Check the server's CapabilityStatement (/metadata) to see which search parameters it actually supports.
What is a FHIR Bundle and what types exist?

A Bundle is a container of resource entries. searchset holds search results. transaction is processed atomically, all or nothing, and can use temporary urn:uuid references between new resources. batch runs each entry independently. document starts with a Composition. message starts with a MessageHeader. history lists versions, and collection is a plain grouping.
What is SMART on FHIR and how do scopes work?

SMART on FHIR is a profile of OAuth2/OIDC for healthcare apps. The app discovers endpoints from .well-known/smart-configuration, runs the authorization code flow with PKCE (EHR or standalone launch), and gets a token with launch context such as the patient ID. Scopes have the form context/Resource.permissions: patient/Observation.read in v1, patient/Observation.rs in v2, user/*.read, and system/*.read for backend services. Add openid fhirUser for identity and offline_access for refresh tokens.
What is US Core?

US Core is the HL7 implementation guide of FHIR R4 profiles that defines the minimum US data (aligned with USCDI). It specifies which elements are required or must be supported, which terminology to use (LOINC, SNOMED CT, RxNorm) and which searches servers must support. Certified EHR APIs are tested against it, so a US Core-conformant client can work with many EHRs with little custom mapping.
Which HIPAA safeguards do you implement as a developer?

Technical safeguards: unique logins and RBAC with least privilege, MFA, session timeouts, audit logs of PHI access and changes, integrity controls, and encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest (encrypted disks, DB and backups, keys in a KMS). On top of that: no PHI in logs, URLs or test data, prepared statements and output escaping, dependency patching, and BAAs with any vendor (cloud, email, AI) that touches PHI. 💡 Also mention the "minimum necessary" principle when designing APIs and reports.
What should an audit log in an EHR capture?

Who (user ID and role), what (action: view, create, update, delete, print, export), which record (patient and resource ID), when (UTC timestamp), where (IP, device, client app), and the outcome (success or denied). Include "break-the-glass" overrides. Logs should be append-only, tamper-evident, retained according to policy, searchable for patient-access reports, and they must not contain more PHI than needed.
How do you escape output and protect forms in OpenEMR code?

Use the core helpers: text() for HTML body text, attr() inside attributes, js_escape() for JavaScript values, and xlt()/xla() to translate and escape in one step. In Twig templates autoescape does this for you. Add a CSRF token (CsrfUtils::collectCsrfToken()) to forms and verify it on submit. Check permissions with the ACL API before reading or writing PHI, and use bound parameters in every SQL call.
Explain the SOAP note.

SOAP is the standard structure for documenting an encounter. Subjective: the patient's own account (chief complaint, HPI, symptoms). Objective: measurable findings (vitals, exam, lab results). Assessment: the clinician's diagnosis or differential. Plan: treatment, prescriptions, orders, education, follow-up. In an EMR, the assessment usually maps to ICD-10 codes and the plan to orders and MedicationRequests.
Walk through a typical outpatient clinical workflow in an EMR.

Scheduling, then eligibility check, then check-in (demographics, insurance, consent), then intake (vitals, medication and allergy reconciliation), then the provider encounter (SOAP note, diagnoses, orders, e-prescriptions), then checkout (follow-up appointment, patient summary or portal access), then coding and charge capture, then claim submission and payment posting. Lab results come back, often over HL7 v2, and are filed and reviewed against the encounter.
What is a CodeableConcept, and why can it hold several codings?

A CodeableConcept represents a coded meaning: an array of coding entries (each with system, code, display) plus optional text. Several codings let the same concept be sent in multiple code systems — for example SNOMED CT for clinical use and ICD-10-CM for billing — or a local code with its standard equivalent. Receivers should match on system + code, never on display text.
How do you prevent two users from overwriting each other's update to a FHIR resource?

Use optimistic locking: the server returns the resource's meta.versionId as an ETag (e.g. W/"3"). The client sends If-Match: W/"3" on its PUT; if someone else updated it first, the server responds 412 Precondition Failed and the client re-reads and merges. This is the FHIR equivalent of JPA's @Version. Version history is available via _history.
What are conditional create and conditional update in FHIR?

Conditional create sends If-None-Exist: identifier=http://hospital/mrn|12345 with a POST, so the server creates the resource only if no match exists — this avoids duplicates when a message is retried. Conditional update is PUT Patient?identifier=...: it updates the single match or creates one if none exists, and fails if several match. Both make integrations idempotent, which matters because interfaces retry.
How would you consume or expose FHIR from a Spring Boot application?

Use HAPI FHIR. As a client: create one FhirContext.forR4() bean (it is expensive and thread-safe), build an IGenericClient, add an auth interceptor with a SMART/OAuth2 token, and use the fluent search API, following Bundle paging links. As a server: either implement IResourceProvider classes over your own database with HAPI's RestfulServer servlet, or deploy the HAPI JPA server. Validate incoming resources against the relevant profiles (US Core or your own).
How do you integrate an HL7 v2 lab feed into a Java system?

Messages usually arrive over MLLP (TCP with start/end framing bytes), often via an interface engine such as Mirth Connect. In Java, use HAPI v2 to parse the ORU^R01 message, read PID for the patient and OBR/OBX for orders and results, and return an ACK (AA accept, AE/AR error/reject) so the sender knows whether to retry. Store or map results to FHIR Observation/DiagnosticReport, match the patient by MRN, and keep the raw message for audit and replay. Make processing idempotent on the message control ID (MSH-10).
How do you handle duplicate patient records?

Prevent them first: search before registration on identifiers and demographics (name, DOB, phone), with fuzzy matching on names. Use an MPI or matching service that scores candidates; auto-link only high-confidence matches and send the rest to a review queue. Merging must keep a full audit trail, re-point encounters, orders and results to the surviving record, and be reversible (unmerge), because a wrong merge mixes two people's clinical data — a patient-safety issue.
What is the difference between de-identification and pseudonymisation?

De-identified data (HIPAA Safe Harbor: remove 18 identifier types; or Expert Determination) is no longer PHI and can be used for analytics with fewer restrictions. Pseudonymised data replaces identifiers with tokens but can be re-linked with a key, so it is still regulated (and is still personal data under GDPR). For dev and test environments, prefer synthetic data (for example Synthea) over masked copies of production.
What is Patient/$everything and when would you use it?

GET Patient/123/$everything is a FHIR operation that returns a Bundle with the patient and all related resources the server holds (encounters, conditions, observations, medications…), optionally limited by _since, _type or date range. It is useful for patient record exports or transferring a chart. For whole populations, use Bulk Data $export instead, which produces NDJSON files asynchronously.
What is CDS Hooks?

A standard for plugging clinical decision support into the EHR workflow. At defined hooks such as patient-view or order-sign, the EHR POSTs context (patient, draft orders, prefetched FHIR data) to a CDS service, which returns cards: information, warnings, suggested actions or a link to launch a SMART app. Examples: drug–allergy interaction warnings, overdue screening reminders. Services must respond fast (sub-second) because they sit in the clinician's workflow.
Besides HIPAA, which regulations might a healthcare app need to consider?

In the US, the 21st Century Cures Act requires certified EHRs to offer standard FHIR APIs and prohibits information blocking (unreasonably preventing access to or exchange of health data); ONC certification criteria define the details. In the EU, GDPR treats health data as a special category requiring explicit legal basis, data minimisation and breach notification within 72 hours. In India, the DPDP Act governs personal data and ABDM defines health IDs (ABHA) and FHIR-based exchange. 💡 Mention whichever applies to the market you worked in, and the controls you implemented.
